questions.questionText: What is the prerequisite condition for binary search and how does it operate in each step?
options: It can be applied to unsorted data and swaps elements until the target reaches the middle.
It needs a linked list and moves sequentially from the start until the target is found.
It works on any collection and selects a random element to compare with the target in each step.
It requires a sorted collection and repeatedly compares the target with the middle element, discarding half of the remaining elements each step.
questions.correctAnswer: It requires a sorted collection and repeatedly compares the target with the middle element, discarding half of the remaining elements each step.
questions.explanation: Binary search only works on collections that are sorted (and allow random access). In each iteration it compares the target with the middle element and eliminates the half of the array that cannot contain the target, thus narrowing the search space.

questions.questionText: During a binary search on the sorted array [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91] for the key 23, after comparing the key with the middle element, which sub-array will be searched next?
options: The middle element 16 is the target
questions.explanation: The middle element of the array (index 4) is 16. Since the target key 23 is greater than 16, binary search discards the left half and continues with the right sub-array that starts at index 5, which is [23, 38, 56, 72, 91].

questions.questionText: Which of the following sequences correctly describes the binary‑search based algorithm to find the median of two sorted arrays A (size m) and B (size n)?
options: Compute mid = (n+m-1)/2, assign i = mid and j = mid, then check if A[i-1] ≤ B[j] and B[j-1] ≤ A[i]; if true, return i as the median index, otherwise repeat with a different mid.
Merge the two arrays linearly until the (m+n)/2‑th element is reached and return that element as the median.
Set i = (m+n)/2, j = i, then compare A[i] with B[j] and increment both i and j by 1 each iteration until A[i] ≤ B[j] and B[j] ≤ A[i] hold, then return A[i] as the median.

Initialize low = 0, high = m. While low ≤ high: set i = (low+high)/2, j = (m+n+1)/2 - i. If i>0 and A[i-1] > B[j], set high = i-1. Else if i<m and B[j-1] > A[i], set low = i+1. Otherwise compute the median from max(A[i-1],B[j-1]) and min(A[i],B[j]) depending on whether (m+n) is odd or even.
questions.correctAnswer: Initialize low = 0, high = m. While low ≤ high: set i = (low+high)/2, j = (m+n+1)/2 - i. If i>0 and A[i-1] > B[j], set high = i-1. Else if i<m and B[j-1] > A[i], set low = i+1. Otherwise compute the median from max(A[i-1],B[j-1]) and min(A[i],B[j]) depending on whether (m+n) is odd or even.
questions.explanation: The binary‑search median algorithm partitions the combined length into two halves using i from A and j from B such that i + j = (m+n+1)/2. By adjusting i based on the cross‑array ordering conditions A[i-1] ≤ B[j] and B[j-1] ≤ A[i], the correct partition is found in O(log min(m,n)) time, after which the median is derived from the bordering elements.
